identity.title: Trace the Page
identity.description: Integrate the module model by tracing user action, browser work, requests/responses, resources, rendering, client-side behavior, and the server boundary.

primaryCapability.statement: Integrate module concepts to trace a system from user action to backend enforcement.

canDo: Place individual components on the web model
likelyMisconceptions: Thinking of frontend problems in isolation from the network or server.

canDo: Identify the earliest failure point in a complex trace
Separate browser behavior from server authorization

learning.targetMentalModel: The page is a system; trace the chain.

experience.startingState: The learner has individual models but hasn't integrated them into a single diagnostic habit.
experience.narrativeContext: Investigating a broken dashboard by tracing the entire system.
experience.primaryInteraction: Analyzing multi-symptom scenarios and identifying root cause boundaries.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner can trace a system flow and identify the most likely boundary for a failure.

content.text:
You are investigating a page that used to work. After an update, users report:

> “The dashboard opens, but the styles are missing and the Save button does nothing.”

You are not allowed to guess. Your job is to trace the system.
content.keyTakeaway: System tracing is the senior way to debug.

activities.title: Interactive System Boundary & Diagnostic Trace
activities.instruction: Trigger interface actions and inspect how browser state, network requests, and styles interact.

content.title: Interactive System Boundary & Diagnostic Trace
content.description: Trigger interface actions and inspect how browser state, network requests, and styles interact.

interactive.caption: Trigger interface actions and inspect how browser state, network requests, and styles interact.

content.prompt: Arrange these pieces into a useful causal trace:

items.text: Browser sends a request for the dashboard document.
Browser requests the stylesheet and JavaScript resources.

feedback.correct: Correct. Start at user action, then request, response, resource retrieval, and final output.
feedback.incorrect: Review the chain of events from previous lessons.

content.question: Given the symptom “dashboard content appears, but styles are missing,” which investigation should happen first?

options.text: Inspect whether the stylesheet request succeeded and whether the browser received usable CSS.

feedback.correct: Correct. The earliest clue points to the stylesheet boundary. Investigate the resource request/response before changing unrelated code.
feedback.incorrect: Which resource is responsible for presentation? Start there.

content.question: The page is styled correctly, but clicking Save produces no visible change. Which investigation order is most sensible?

options.text: Check the CSS color, then the server database, then the keyboard.
Check whether the browser loaded the JavaScript, whether the click behavior is connected, and whether the browser-side code runs as expected.
Assume the server is broken before checking the browser-side path.

feedback.correct: Correct. The symptom is a client-side interaction problem. Start with the browser-side code path that should react to the click.
feedback.incorrect: Where does the 'Save' behavior live? Start your trace there.

content.question: The Delete button is hidden for non-admin users. A developer says: “Security problem solved.” What is your response?

options.text: Correct. A hidden button means the action cannot happen.
Not enough. The server must enforce authorization even if the UI hides the button.
The browser should contain the admin password.

feedback.correct: Correct. The UI can guide users, but it does not establish authorization.
feedback.incorrect: Is a hidden button a real security boundary?

content.prompt:
Write a 5–7 sentence explanation for this page:

“A user opens /dashboard. The dashboard page appears. A stylesheet request fails. The Save button has JavaScript attached, but the server returns an authorization error when saving.”

Your explanation should identify: what the browser requested, what failure explains the visual problem, what work happens in the browser, what work crosses to the server, and why a visible button is not proof of authorization.
content.sampleResponse: The user enters the dashboard URL, so the browser requests the dashboard resource. The dashboard response arrives and the browser renders the document. The stylesheet request fails, so the browser has the structure but not the intended presentation. The Save behavior can run in the browser, but saving crosses the browser/server boundary when it sends a request. The server evaluates whether the operation is allowed and returns an authorization error. The presence of a visible button does not prove the user is authorized because the server must enforce that rule.
guidelines: Separate browser behavior from server behavior
Treat authorization as a server-enforced concern

content.question: You are now looking at an image gallery instead of a dashboard. One image is broken. Another loads but appears stretched. A “Favorite” button changes to “Saved” locally but does not persist after refresh. Match the investigation.

options.text: 1. Broken image → check request/response; 2. Stretched → check layout; 3. No persist → trace browser change + save request.
1. Replace gallery; 2. Change monitor; 3. Use a different browser.

feedback.correct: Correct. The surface changed. The reasoning model did not.
feedback.incorrect: Focus on the boundaries: resource retrieval, rendering, and persistence.

content.text:
You are ready to leave Module 0.1 when you can do all three without copying the previous answers:

**1. Trace:** Explain the path from user action to visible result.
**2. Diagnose:** Identify the earliest changed boundary when a symptom appears.
**3. Explain:** Distinguish browser-side work from server-side work and explain why security-sensitive authorization must be enforced on the server.
content.keyTakeaway: The page is a system. Trace the chain.

takeaways: Mental model: The page is a system. The user triggers events. The browser runs work. The browser exchanges information with servers. Resources arrive. The browser processes them. The final interface is the visible consequence of those steps.
Senior habit: Do not ask “What looks broken?” first. Ask “What was the first step that stopped behaving as expected?”
